paragraphs.text: A plan to take Harlow Fresh Markets' operating margin from 1.0% back to 3.0% by FY2028, and what to do first
Presented by Dana Whitfield, Chief Executive Officer
All figures in $ millions unless stated. Fiscal years end in January. Based only on the board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data).

slides.title: Margin is falling because of promotions, shrink and e-commerce delivery, not wages; fixing those first gets Harlow to ~3% by FY2028

paragraphs.text: Margin is falling because of promotions, shrink and e-commerce delivery, not wages; fixing those first gets Harlow to ~3% by FY2028
Operating margin fell from 3.4% to 1.0% in two years (FY2023–FY2025); operating income fell from $47.9M to $15.3M while sales grew 6%.
About 80% of the fall is gross margin (deeper promotions, more shrink) and e-commerce fulfilment. Store labor explains 13%: wages rose 9.4%, but 6% fewer hours per sales dollar offset most of it.
E-commerce loses ~$10M a year once third-party delivery and sales taken from our own stores are counted.

Replace the 8% across-the-board labor cut with six actions: cut loss-making promotions, restore fresh and receiving routines to cut shrink, reprice delivery, grow private label, exit the nine loss-making stores, and target labor savings where hours are heaviest.
Result: ~$39M operating income (2.8%) in FY2028 on cautious assumptions; $5.5M of named stretch levers take it to 3.1%. Management's draft plan reaches ~1.5%.
Start with promotions, delivery pricing and shrink: fast, low-capital, partly tested. They should lift FY2026 to ~$24–28M, above the $20M covenant.
Approve the plan in place of the draft labor-cut plan, and launch wave 1 now.
Approve in principle the exit of the three loss-making stores whose leases run beyond 2027 ($7.5M one-time); store-by-store cases come to the next board meeting.
Keep home delivery, but repriced, with delivered-order growth on hold until each order covers its cost.
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data)

slides.title: Operating margin fell 2.4 points in two years; gross margin and e-commerce explain about 80% of the fall, store labor about 13%

paragraphs.text: Operating margin fell 2.4 points in two years; gross margin and e-commerce explain about 80% of the fall, store labor about 13%
Operating margin, % of sales, FY2023 → FY2025 (points of sales)
Gross margin and e-commerce together took 1.86 of the 2.36 points lost. Both are commercial and operating choices we control.
E-commerce fulfilment nearly tripled as a share of sales: orders rose from 453k to 1.33M and home delivery's share of orders rose from 45% to 58%.
Store labor rose only 0.3 points of sales despite 9.4% wage inflation (page 5). It is a real pressure, but not the main one.
Other SG&A held steady at 4.7% of sales.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 1. Change in each line as a % of sales, FY2023 to FY2025; $ effect valued at FY2025 sales of $1,503M. Sales growth at the FY2023 margin added ~$2.8M. Points may not sum exactly because of rounding.

slides.title: Deeper promotions and higher shrink cut gross margin by 1.2 points; private-label growth won back only 0.2

paragraphs.text: Deeper promotions and higher shrink cut gross margin by 1.2 points; private-label growth won back only 0.2
Gross margin change FY2023 → FY2025, points of sales ($M)
Promotions are not paying for themselves
38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money, even after counting the extra units they sold.
Vendors now fund less of each markdown: 46% in FY2025, down from 55% in FY2023.
Deeper promotions did not fix price perception: 41% of customers now call Harlow "more expensive" (33% in FY2023). Their top reasons to shop with us are fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%).

The category team's evidence (deep-promotion stores: comparable sales +1.8% vs +0.2%) measures sales, not profit. Each extra point of promotional share costs 0.14% of sales in margin, so it needs ~0.7% more sales at 20% contribution just to break even.
The three drivers in the pack add up exactly to the 1.02-point fall, so nothing material is missing from this explanation.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Tables 1–2 and sections 5 and 9. Effect = change in share of sales × margin gap (promotions −14 pts, private label +12 pts); shrink effect = change in shrink % of sales. $ at FY2025 sales.

slides.title: Wages rose 9%, but productivity absorbed most of it; cutting hours further risks more shrink, which is already highest in the leanest stores

paragraphs.text: Wages rose 9%, but productivity absorbed most of it; cutting hours further risks more shrink, which is already highest in the leanest stores
Store labor as % of sales: what changed, FY2023 → FY2025
Shrink, % of sales, FY2025, by store labor quartile (chain average 2.6%)
Net change in labor % of sales
Implication for management's 8% hour cut (~$14.5M a year)

It would take the chain to ~6.1 hours per $1,000 of sales. The last 6% reduction came with shrink rising 0.5 points (~$7.5M a year), and managers in the leanest stores say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days. Each 0.1 point of shrink costs ~$1.5M, so the cut could give back half its savings, before any effect on checkout waits or stock-outs.
Better: target hours where labor is heaviest and shrink lowest (Q3–Q4), and protect fresh and receiving tasks in the leanest stores.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Tables 3–4 and section 6. Labor % of sales = wage × hours per $1,000 of sales. Quartiles rank stores by labor hours per $1,000 of sales. The shrink pattern is a correlation across stores, not proof of cause.

slides.title: E-commerce loses about $10M a year once delivery costs and sales taken from our stores are counted, not the 6.1% profit reported

paragraphs.text: E-commerce loses about $10M a year once delivery costs and sales taken from our stores are counted, not the 6.1% profit reported
Why the reported 6.1% margin is wrong
It leaves out third-party delivery, which finance books separately: $10.7M of cost less $2.4M of fees, a net $8.3M in FY2025.
It counts every online sale as new. Customers say 70% of what they buy online they would otherwise have bought in a Harlow store, where we already earn that margin.
The conclusion holds even if the survey is wrong: at today's costs e-commerce breaks even only if more than 70% of its sales are new to Harlow.
Click-and-collect is close to break-even; home delivery is the problem. Delivery is free above $75 and the average basket is $96, so most delivered orders pay no fee.
Total e-commerce: −$10.4M a year, versus +$7.8M (6.1% of $127.8M sales) in the e-commerce team's update

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 5 and sections 7 and 10. New contribution = $96 basket × 30% genuinely new sales (survey: 70% would otherwise be bought in a Harlow store) × $0.20 contribution per new $. FY2025: 1,331k orders, 58% delivered.

slides.title: The tested delivery pricing saves ~$2.5M a year and keeps 98% of e-commerce sales; the 2026 contract renewal is the next lever

paragraphs.text: The tested delivery pricing saves ~$2.5M a year and keeps 98% of e-commerce sales; the 2026 contract renewal is the next lever
Roll out the tested pricing chain-wide now. No capital needed; most lost delivery orders switch to click-and-collect.
Use the 2026 contract renewal. The provider's proposed 3% rise would cost ~$0.3M a year; each $1 off the rate per delivered order is worth ~$0.7M.

Keep delivery, but stop it growing at a loss. Even after the fee change a delivered order loses ~$9, so we hold delivered volume flat, steer customers to click-and-collect, and test the next fee step.
This keeps the owners' commitment to delivery; the draft plan's freeze alone would leave the ~$10M loss in place.
Saving $3.0M less ≤$0.5M contribution on lost sales = ~$2.5M a year net

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 5 and section 7. Fee test: 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025; results applied to FY2025 volumes. Lost contribution assumes all lost e-commerce sales leave Harlow at 20% contribution (cautious).

slides.title: Exiting the nine loss-making stores adds ~$6.6M a year; six can close as their leases expire, without a board vote

paragraphs.text: Exiting the nine loss-making stores adds ~$6.6M a year; six can close as their leases expire, without a board vote
Annual operating income effect of exiting all nine stores ($M)
Use each lease expiry to renegotiate rent first; close only if four-wall EBITDA stays negative.
Ask the board to approve in principle the three longer-lease exits now, with a store-by-store case at the next meeting.
Exits land across FY2027–FY2028 as leases end, so the full run-rate may come only in FY2029.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), Table 6. Split between the 6 and 3 stores assumes losses and sales are spread evenly (the pack gives only combined figures). Closure costs other than lease exits are not in the pack.

slides.title: The draft labor-led plan reaches only ~1.5% margin by FY2028 because it leaves the largest causes of the decline untouched

paragraphs.text: The draft labor-led plan reaches only ~1.5% margin by FY2028 because it leaves the largest causes of the decline untouched
Restore produce rotation and receiving checks; 2.6% → 2.3%
Reprice delivery, renegotiate contract, steer to collect
8% fewer hours in the most labor-heavy half only
Private-label growth (18.5% → 20% of sales) is a further lever in the recommended plan only.
Draft plan range: 2.0% if the wage rise is ignored; ~1.0% if shrink rises as it did after the last hour cuts.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data). Management plan: 8% fewer hours ($14.5M), e-commerce frozen, all 58 stores kept (FY2025 sales base). Both plans absorb the 2027 minimum-wage rise (+4%, assumed to apply to all store labor). Recommended plan detail on page 10.

slides.title: The plan rebuilds operating income to ~$39M (2.8%) by FY2028; $5.5M of named stretch levers would take it past 3.0%

paragraphs.text: The plan rebuilds operating income to ~$39M (2.8%) by FY2028; $5.5M of named stretch levers would take it past 3.0%
Operating income bridge, FY2025 actual → FY2028 plan ($M)

Rate levers valued on a FY2028 sales base of $1,415M (FY2025 sales less the nine stores, plus recaptured sales; no market growth assumed). Labor: 8% fewer hours in the most labor-heavy half of stores (~4% of chain hours). Wage rise: +4% on all store labor (cautious). Stretch: promotions to 24% (+$2.0M), shrink to 2.1% (+$2.8M), $1 lower delivery rate (+$0.7M). Vendor-funding recovery not counted.

slides.title: Start with three fast, low-capital moves: they deliver about half of the plan's gross gains and protect the FY2026 covenant

paragraphs.text: Start with three fast, low-capital moves: they deliver about half of the plan's gross gains and protect the FY2026 covenant
Cut loss-making promotions (share 29% → 25%), holding price where ValuMart competes
Medium: 38% of events lose money; traffic risk near ValuMart
Roll out tested delivery pricing; renegotiate the delivery contract
Restore produce rotation and receiving checks in the leanest stores
Medium: shrink 3.1% vs 2.3% across labor quartiles
Cut hours 8% in the most labor-heavy half of stores; protect fresh and receiving
Medium: watch shrink and checkout waits
Grow private label from 18.5% to 20% of sales
Medium: +12 pts margin; continues the trend
Exit six loss-making stores at lease expiry
Exit three loss-making stores with longer leases
Wave 1 = $14.6M of the $30.5M gross gains (48%). The 2027 wage rise (−$6.8M) offsets the labor lever.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data). FY2028 run-rate impact. Confidence reflects the strength of evidence in the pack. One-time costs other than the $7.5M lease exits are not in the pack and need a CFO estimate.

slides.title: Wave 1 should lift FY2026 operating income to ~$24–28M, above the $20M covenant; identified one-time costs are $7.5M of the $25M budget

paragraphs.text: Wave 1 should lift FY2026 operating income to ~$24–28M, above the $20M covenant; identified one-time costs are $7.5M of the $25M budget
Six store exits at lease expiry
Identified: $7.5M for the three lease exits.
Not yet costed: closing the six other stores, shrink controls, private-label development. The CFO will cost these before the next board meeting.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data). FY2026 in-year estimates assume: half the promotion reset (2 pts), 9 months of delivery pricing, a 0.15-pt shrink reduction, half a year of targeted labor savings and +0.5 pt private label, valued at FY2025 sales, with the underlying business holding at FY2025 levels.

slides.title: Five risks could knock the plan off course; each has an early warning sign and an agreed response

paragraphs.text: Five risks could knock the plan off course; each has an early warning sign and an agreed response
Early warning sign we will track
Cutting promotions loses traffic to ValuMart (11 stores opened in our trade areas since 2023)
Weekly traffic and comparable sales in stores within three miles of a ValuMart (already −4.2% in FY2025)
Cut first outside ValuMart areas; where traffic falls, put part of the saving into private label and everyday prices
Fewer hours raise shrink or hurt service
Shrink % by store; checkout waits; stock-outs
Protect fresh and receiving hours; pause cuts in any store whose shrink rises 0.2 pts
E-commerce sales against the test's −2%; switching to click-and-collect
Adjust fee and threshold; the test showed most delivery customers switch rather than leave
Costs rise further: delivery contract (+3% proposed), minimum wage (+4% in 2027)
Contract terms at renewal; wage settlements
Plan already absorbs the full wage rise; rebid delivery if the provider will not hold rates
E-commerce cannibalisation estimate rests on a survey
Basket and store-visit data for online customers
Low exposure: e-commerce loses money unless over 70% of its sales are new
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data), sections 9 and 11.

Labor hours per $1,000 of sales, by quartile
Brief the lender on the FY2026 outlook and plan.

Promotion reset, chain-wide delivery pricing and contract renegotiation, fresh and receiving routines. No significant capital.

$7.5M one-time cost, ~$2.2M a year, ~3.4-year payback. Store-by-store cases at the next board meeting for the formal vote.

slides.title: Key calculations and assumptions behind the plan

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX A: HOW THE NUMBERS WERE BUILT
Key calculations and assumptions behind the plan
Promo share +5.0 pts × −14 pts; private label +1.5 pts × +12 pts; shrink +0.5 pts
Delivered −9%, collect +14%, fee $6.40 → cost $15.1M; minus ≤$0.5M on the 2% of sales lost
−4 pts × 14 pts; +1.5 pts × 12 pts; −0.3 pts; each on $1,415M
Store labor scaled to $171M; 4% of hours saved; +4% wage on all store labor
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data). All lever values are run-rate annual effects on operating income.

slides.title: Where the pack is thin, we chose cautious assumptions; these are the ones that matter most

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX B: DATA LIMITS AND CHOICES MADE
Where the pack is thin, we chose cautious assumptions; these are the ones that matter most
Shrink and labor: the quartile pattern is a correlation across stores, not proof that fewer hours cause shrink.
Cannibalisation: the 70% figure is what customers say in a survey (n = 2,300). The conclusion holds unless over 70% of online sales are new.
Fee test: 4 stores over 10 weeks; chain-wide response may differ.
Promotions: the valuation assumes promotional sales move to regular price rather than disappear; we stop at 4 of the ~11 points of share in money-losing events.
Stores: only combined figures for the nine stores are available; the 6/3 split is pro rata.
No market growth in the FY2028 sales base; margin gains come only from the actions.
Full wage pass-through: the 2027 rise is applied to all store labor, though not every employee is on the minimum wage. Partial pass-through would be upside.
Vendor funding recovery (46% back towards 55%) is not counted.

Timing: the pack treats FY2026 as the first plan year. If FY2026 is largely booked by the time of the meeting, the covenant view on page 12 should be replaced with the actual result before it goes to the lender.
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data).
